Nevertheless, while 3000 years is more than enough to build up a culture of "us" vs "them", I don't believe it is sufficient for instrumental, evolutionary changes in behavior. Accounting for environmental epigenetics, if you take one population from one region and swap it for another in another region, in a generation or two, I suspect you'd undo most all of the on-average-measurably-different behavioral changes made in the past 3000 stable years. Assuming, of course, no multigenerational cultural barriers.

Does the isolation of communities influence genetics? Of course. But it's at a scale much longer than can account for perceived behavioral differences in various people groups. And humans are migrators, and borders do not hold us. After all, we are something like 99.5% genetically identical.
